content: A noticeable increase in waist size, along with bloating and abdominal distension, may indicate an underlying organic disease. These symptoms should be carefully evaluated, with potential organic causes considered first in the differential diagnosis. Bloating is one of the most common complaints among patients with gastrointestinal disorders, with constipation being the leading cause. Other conditions associated with bloating include irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), gastroparesis, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO), and gynecological disorders. The exact pathophysiology of bloating remains poorly understood. Proposed mechanisms include visceral hypersensitivity, abnormal abdominal wall-diaphragmatic reflexes, poor digestion of fermentable carbohydrates, and alterations in the gut microbiome. A thorough patient history and physical examination are essential for evaluation, with organic disorders needing to be ruled out. Management strategies typically involve dietary modifications, behavioral therapy, microbiome modulation, and medical therapy. Historically, bloating has been described in various ways. In 1891, Bernheim documented a woman who likened her symptoms to going up and down like an accordion. Kaplan, in 1900, referred to the condition as ventre en accordéon. Sir James Y. Simpson was the first to describe a non-gaseous form of bloating. In the 19th century, European physicians would puncture the intestines with a trocar in cases of suspected obstruction, discovering that no gas was present in cases of hysteric bloating. Bloating was also once considered a tumor that disappeared under anesthesia and reappeared when the patient regained consciousness. Lordosis associated with bloating was described by Krukenberg in 1884, and in 1949, Alvarez of the Mayo Clinic documented bloating in a woman with a psychiatric condition. There is no established classification system for bloating. However, several mechanisms have been proposed: 1. Abnormal Gut Microbiota: The type of gas produced by colonic microflora is linked to bloating. Methanogenic flora has been implicated, with studies showing increased bloating in individuals with low methane production after ingesting sorbitol and fiber. 2. Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO): Bacterial fermentation and subsequent gas production are potential causes of bloating in IBS patients. 3. Intestinal Gas Accumulation: Increased intestinal gas levels are associated with bloating. After a large meal, postprandial gas volume in the pelvic colon can increase by 65%. During fasting, the gastrointestinal tract produces approximately 100 mL of gas, distributed across various regions of the gut. 4. Altered Gut Motility: Disorders affecting gut motility, such as intestinal dysmotility, impair the evacuation of excess gas during fasting and after meals. 5. Abnormal Abdominal-Diaphragmatic Reflexes: Abnormal reflexes involving increased anterior abdominal wall tone and diaphragmatic relaxation have been observed in individuals with bloating. 6. Visceral Hypersensitivity: Patients with functional gastrointestinal disorders may perceive normal stimuli or small variations in gut gas content as bloating. The autonomic nervous system may also play a role, with sympathetic activation heightening the perception of intestinal distension. 7. Food Intolerance and Carbohydrate Malabsorption: High-FODMAP diets can lead to prolonged hydrogen production, colonic distension from fermentation, increased colonic fluid delivery due to osmotic load, and gastrointestinal symptoms. 8. Hard Stool/Constipation: Rectal distension from retained feces alters gut motility and increases bacterial fermentation. The most common causes of bloating include constipation, pregnancy, IBS, celiac disease, lactose and fructose intolerance, pancreatic insufficiency, gastroparesis, diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, scleroderma, chronic idiopathic pseudo-obstruction, SIBO, acute gastroenteritis, gastric or ovarian malignancy, and ascites. Differentiating bloating from other conditions is crucial. Conditions to consider include lactose and fructose intolerance, celiac disease, pancreatic insufficiency, IBS, functional dyspepsia, functional bloating, constipation, diabetes, scleroderma, pseudo-obstruction (acute or chronic), gastroparesis, acute adynamic ileus, gastric outlet obstruction, small bowel obstruction, SMA syndrome, colonic obstruction, volvulus, gastrointestinal or ovarian malignancy, ascites, pregnancy, and obesity. Epidemiologically, 15-30% of the U.S. population reports experiencing bloating. A telephone survey found a prevalence of 16% among U.S. adults, with women more likely than men to report symptoms. There is no racial predilection for bloating. Risk factors include chewing gum, consuming hard candy, and drinking carbonated beverages like soda or beer. Foods such as leafy greens, beans, and bran can produce excess bowel gas. Dairy products may cause bloating and flatulence in lactose-intolerant individuals. Routine screening for bloating is not recommended due to insufficient evidence. The natural history of bloating often involves heightened sensitivity to gaseous distension or exaggerated motor responses to normal gas volumes. While bloating is typically benign, it can occasionally indicate severe conditions like intestinal obstruction or malignancy. Patients with mild functional bloating may only require reassurance of its benign nature. Diagnosis involves the Rome IV criteria, which require recurrent bloating or distension at least one day per week for three months, with symptom onset at least six months prior. A detailed history should assess symptom onset, dietary triggers, diurnal variation, and associated symptoms like constipation, diarrhea, abdominal pain, or postprandial fullness. Functional bloating often follows a diurnal pattern, worsening after meals and improving overnight. Physical examination findings may include abdominal distension with or without altered bowel sounds. Alarm features such as occult fecal blood, cutaneous findings (e.g., sclerodactyly in scleroderma, dermatitis herpetiformis in celiac disease), neuropathy, cachexia, jaundice, or palpable masses suggest underlying organic disease. Laboratory tests may include: Complete blood count to evaluate for anemia. Serologies for celiac disease (anti-tissue transglutaminase, endomysial antibodies, deamidated gliadin peptide antibodies). Hydrogen breath test for SIBO and lactose intolerance. Thyroid function tests. Fasting cortisol levels. Antinuclear antibodies and scleroderma antibodies for collagen vascular disease. Antineuronal antibodies for paraneoplastic visceral neuropathy. Stool analysis for Giardia antigen testing. Imaging studies may include: Abdominal X-rays to rule out intestinal obstruction. Abdominal or pelvic ultrasound to evaluate for ascites or ovarian cancer. CT scans to rule out intestinal obstruction. Upper GI endoscopy for alarm features like weight loss, abdominal pain, dysphagia, heartburn, or regurgitation. Treatment involves education, addressing associated disorders, and behavioral therapy. Patients should minimize air swallowing and avoid gum chewing, smoking, carbonated drinks, and rapid food or liquid consumption. Diaphragmatic breathing exercises can reduce postprandial intragastric pressure and improve symptoms. For refractory symptoms, baclofen may be prescribed to reduce transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxations and suppress swallowing rates. Surgical intervention is not recommended for bloating management. There are no established measures for the primary or secondary prevention of bloating.
